metadata.title: What drives the performance of Chinese urban and rural secondary schools: A machine learning approach using PISA 2018

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 micro-level data for China, restricted to students from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, and then aggregates student-level information to the school level for the outcome. The manuscript states that “information at the student level is weighted averaged by school level and matched to school-level data,” but it does not report the use of PISA student/sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or any replicate-weight procedure. Because the predictive modeling is implemented via linear regression and XGBoost with a random 80:20 train/test split, the paper does not describe complex-survey variance estimation; this suggests weights were not applied in the ML estimation stage (or are only used for the school-level averaging step). No explicit missing-data handling or outlier trimming rules are reported, so the analytic sample is best interpreted as the set of schools after excluding those with insufficient information.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper models school-level average mathematics, science, and reading scores (TSCORE) and does not describe how PISA plausible values (PVs) were handled when constructing the school-level outcome. Because PV handling is not documented, it is unclear whether PVs were averaged, combined using Rubin’s rules, or replaced by a single score; this is a reporting gap given that PISA achievement is typically PV-based. The manuscript also does not report any explicit missing-data strategy for questionnaire or school variables, so missingness treatment cannot be verified.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA 2018 micro-level data for China, restricted to students from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang. Excludes schools with insufficient information, then constructs a school-level outcome as the average score of mathematics, science, and reading. Student-level information is weighted-averaged to the school level and matched to school-level data; the final analytic unit for modeling is the school (best vs worst schools within urban and rural areas).

confounders_identified.variable_name: Two or more schools in area

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 China (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) — school-level average mathematics/science/reading
main_findings.target_variable: School academic performance (TSCORE) for best vs benchmark (urban)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear regression outperforms XGBoost; no numeric accuracy/R² reported for the final model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 China the study leveraged meta-cognition (METASPAM), class size (CLSIZE), socioeconomic status (ESCS), competitiveness perception (PERCOMP), and ability grouping (SCHABILICLASS) to predict school academic performance (TSCORE) for the best school in urban areas versus the benchmark school, finding that intermediate learning outcomes and student characteristics (especially METASPAM) contribute positively while ability grouping negatively impacts performance. This indicates that strengthening students’ credibility-assessment meta-cognition and addressing socioeconomic and classroom-size conditions may be more effective than ability-grouping policies for improving urban school achievement, though the paper’s SHAP-based causal-structure interpretation is predictive rather than proof of causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 China (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) — school-level average mathematics/science/reading
main_findings.target_variable: School academic performance (TSCORE) for worst vs benchmark (urban)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear regression outperforms XGBoost; no numeric accuracy/R² reported for the final model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 China the study leveraged learning time (TMINS), parental emotional support (EMOSUPS), socioeconomic status (ESCS), grade repetition (REPEAT), and expected occupational status (BSMJ) to predict school academic performance (TSCORE) for the worst school in urban areas versus the benchmark school, finding that poorer intermediate learning outcomes and lower student characteristics reduce achievement, with grade repetition lowering performance by 23.02 points. This indicates that urban underperforming schools may benefit from targeted grade-repetition reduction, family-support interventions, and learning-time supports to improve intermediate learning outcomes, while the reported point differences are model-based contributions rather than causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 China (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) — school-level average mathematics/science/reading
main_findings.target_variable: School academic performance (TSCORE) for best vs benchmark (rural)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear regression outperforms XGBoost; no numeric accuracy/R² reported for the final model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 China the study leveraged school ICT availability (RATCMP1), student behavior hindering learning (STUBEHA), admission policy complexity (ADMISSION), home ICT resources (ICTRES), and ability grouping (SCHABILICLASS) to predict school academic performance (TSCORE) for the best school in rural areas versus the benchmark school, finding that school characteristics (especially ICT and learning environment quality) are more important in rural areas and that insufficient home ICT (ICTRES) harms performance while greater computer availability at school (RATCMP1) compensates. This indicates that rural achievement gains may require both home-to-school ICT support and improvements in the learning environment, though the study’s causal-structure framing relies on model-based feature contributions rather than randomized policy evaluation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 China (Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Zhejiang) — school-level average mathematics/science/reading
main_findings.target_variable: School academic performance (TSCORE) for worst vs benchmark (rural)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear regression outperforms XGBoost; no numeric accuracy/R² reported for the final model.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 China the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS), learning time (TMINS), parental emotional support (EMOSUPS), home ICT resources (ICTRES), and school computer availability (RATCMP1) to predict school academic performance (TSCORE) for the worst school in rural areas versus the benchmark school, finding that these factors negatively affect intermediate learning outcomes and academic performance, consistent with the urban pattern, and that lack of ICT resources is a key driver. This indicates that rural policy should prioritize ICT subsidies for homes and schools and also address family and learning-time supports to prevent intermediate learning outcomes from deteriorating, while causality cannot be established from observational ML contributions.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 micro-level data for China, restricted to students from Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, and models school-level average mathematics, science, and reading performance (TSCORE). The analytic unit is the school: student-level variables are weighted-averaged to the school level, schools with insufficient information are excluded, and urban vs rural “best” and “worst” schools are compared against a benchmark school (581 points). The authors fit linear regression and compare it to XGBoost, reporting that linear regression outperforms nonlinear models, but they do not provide numeric predictive metrics (e.g., R²/accuracy) for the final model. Feature contributions are interpreted using Shapley flow/values under a causal-structure assumption, with notable point differences such as grade repetition reducing performance by 23.02 points in urban worst schools. Limitations include lack of documented PV handling and missing-data strategy, and SHAP-based contributions are not equivalent to causal identification.
